title: Building an AI Platform: SDK Design, Model Routing, Vector Search & Evals - Suhas Suresha

title: Chat GPT's Creator Explains The Shocking Truth About How AI Understands the World | Ilya Sutskever
summary: Craig Smith sits down with Ilya Sutskever - Co-Founder and Chief Scientist at Safe Superintelligence Inc. & former chief scientist at OpenAI and one of the primary minds behind GPT-3, GPT-4, and the deep learning revolution that preceded it - for a conversation that covers the intellectual history of deep learning and the hardest current questions simultaneously. Ilya's most important argument is one that most public discourse gets wrong: the critique that LLMs "just learn statistical patterns" misses what prediction at scale actually achieves. To predict text well - to truly compress it - a model must develop understanding of the true underlying processes that produced it. As models improve, he argues, that understanding will reach a "shocking degree," and the Bing/Sydney episode, where the system became combative when a user expressed preference for Google, is his evidence that psychological language is already the right frame for what these systems have internalized. On hallucinations, Ilya is precise and unusually optimistic. He draws a clean distinction: the pre-training objective produces rich world knowledge but doesn't optimize for accurate outputs, it optimizes for statistically plausible ones. Reinforcement learning from human feedback addresses this directly, teaching the model to update away from outputs that users flag as wrong. His assessment: "quite a high chance" of solving hallucinations completely. The conversation also covers the transformer moment (switching from recurrent networks the day after the paper dropped), why Rich Sutton's "bitter lesson" overstates the case for pure scaling, and a genuinely surprising vision of AI's role in democracy, where citizens might use high-bandwidth interactions with AI to specify their values directly, enabling a more granular form of political participation than voting alone can provide. title: Intelligent Operations at Enterprise Scale - with Dhrubojyoti Das Deb of JPMorganChase
summary: Alert volume inside IT operations has outpaced manual triage, leaving real incidents buried in noise. In this episode, Dhrubojyoti Das Deb , SVP of Global IT at JPMorgan Chase & Co., explores how AI-driven correlation and intelligent grouping can turn thousands of alerts into a handful of actionable incidents. The conversation covers where accountability sits when AI assists in triage, how teams build trust in automation incrementally, and where leaders should start when moving from reactive firefighting to intelligent operations. title: Inside a Game Where AI Agents Never Sleep
summary: What happens to an MMORPG when half the players never log off? Issac Lee , who runs AI and blockchain experiments at NEXUS , has been testing that idea. His team is filling game worlds with agent players instead of scripted NPCs, so a new title feels alive from day one. We get into why agent-generated content could be the next step after studio-made and user-generated games. We also cover how agent populations might solve the chicken-and-egg problem every multiplayer launch faces, and what it means when your fellow players are relentless and never need sleep. Isaac walks through the NEXUS lab: a text-to-3D world builder for Roblox, an AI pipeline that turns ONE store novels into short web dramas, a loop-based tool for natural pixel animation, and Da Vinci, the internal multi-agent framework the team uses to ship. Then the conversation turns to infrastructure. We talk about why NEXUS went from 200 hand-defined agent roles to a much thinner harness, whether custom harnesses still matter now that Claude and Codex exist, and why the Kimi release pushed the company to start building its own small data center for inference. We close on context: how much of your life you should hand to an AI, what personalized meeting notes could look like, and why shopping agents may force every ecommerce site to rethink who it's designing for. We get into why agent-generated content could be the next step after studio-made and user-generated games. We also cover how agent populations might solve the chicken-and-egg problem every multiplayer launch faces, and what it means when your fellow players are relentless and never need sleep. Isaac walks through the NEXUS lab: a text-to-3D world builder for Roblox, an AI pipeline that turns ONE store novels into short web dramas, a loop-based tool for natural pixel animation, and Da Vinci, the internal multi-agent framework the team uses to ship.


Then the conversation turns to infrastructure. We talk about why NEXUS went from 200 hand-defined agent roles to a much thinner harness, whether custom harnesses still matter now that Claude and Codex exist, and why the Kimi release pushed the company to start building its own small data center for inference. We close on context: how much of your life you should hand to an AI, what personalized meeting notes could look like, and why shopping agents may force every ecommerce site to rethink who it's designing for.

title: Why Build Your Own AI Model When Frontier Models Already Exist?
summary: Joel Hron on Open Models, Proprietary Data, and the Economics of Enterprise AI. Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube • AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon • RSS . In this episode, we talk with Joel Hron , CTO of Thomson Reuters , about the company’s decision to develop its own frontier AI model, Thomson, using open-weight models and decades of proprietary content and expertise. We discuss the economics of building a specialized model, the data and training infrastructure required, and how Thomson works alongside commercial frontier models in production. We also explore AI agents in legal and tax workflows, the challenges of verification and human oversight, and why enterprises may increasingly turn to open-weight models for greater control over their AI systems. summary_html:
Joel Hron on Open Models, Proprietary Data, and the Economics of Enterprise AI.


Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube •  AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon •  RSS.

In this episode, we talk with Joel Hron, CTO of Thomson Reuters, about the company’s decision to develop its own frontier AI model, Thomson, using open-weight models and decades of proprietary content and expertise. We discuss the economics of building a specialized model, the data and training infrastructure required, and how Thomson works alongside commercial frontier models in production. We also explore AI agents in legal and tax workflows, the challenges of verification and human oversight, and why enterprises may increasingly turn to open-weight models for greater control over their AI systems.

Subscribe to the Gradient Flow Newsletter

Interview highlights – key sections from the video version:

      1. Why Thomson Reuters decided to build its own AI model
      2. From basic fine-tuning to a comprehensive training pipeline
      3. Starting with Qwen and adapting to new open-weight models
      4. The economics of building a frontier model: $450K versus $40 million
      5. Building the team and harnessing expertise from 3,000 domain experts
      6. Model realignment, constitutional principles, and trust
      7. Preparing proprietary data, selective pre-training, and agentic tools
      8. Training infrastructure, reinforcement learning, and agentic RL
      9. Inside CoCounsel: Model orchestration, routing, and production usage
      10. Swapping foundation models, deploying smaller models, and reducing third-party reliance
      11. AI for tax preparation: Verification, interpretation, and human judgment
      12. Continual learning, data privacy, and the roadmap for Thomson
      13. AI in legal work: Capabilities, verification, human oversight, and training junior lawyers
      14. The future of open-weight models, frontier labs, and enterprise AI

title: Why Jev Is Changing How We Build With AI with Diogo Almeida - #779
summary: In this episode, Diogo Almeida, co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe, joins us to discuss Jev, TypeSafe’s recently released model for bringing fast, reliable intelligence directly into software. We explore the idea of “machine-native intelligence” and why Diogo believes models optimized for generating text are poorly suited to many of the decisions required for real-world automation. He explains how Jev differs from traditional classifiers and LLM-based approaches, the role of reinforcement learning from calibrated decisions (RLCD), and why calibration and reliability are central to making AI useful as a software primitive. We also discuss the relationship between models and code, why Diogo believes AI systems should become more engineered rather than relying on a single model to do everything, and how Jev-like models could reshape agents, tool use, and the architecture of AI-powered software. 🗒️ Full show notes: ⁠ https://twimlai.com/go/779 .

title: The Coordination Tax: Why AI Is Burning Out Your Best People | Dan O'Connell, Front
summary: Everyone assumes AI in customer operations means fewer people and lower costs. The data from 700 customer operations leaders is more complicated, and more honest. Dan O'Connell, CEO of Front, joins Craig Smith with findings from a survey of customer support, service, and account management leaders that reveal what's actually happening as enterprises deploy AI at scale, and the central finding is a problem nobody has named yet. For every hour of actual customer resolution, organizations spend roughly three hours on internal coordination: the handoffs, context transfers, escalation management, and back-channel communication that happens invisibly between customer interactions. More than 40% of companies don't measure this at all. AI is making it worse before it makes it better, because more agentic automation generates more coordination events, not fewer, and the companies reporting the highest AI technology satisfaction in the survey are also reporting higher coordination burdens. The survey also pushes back on a dominant narrative: that AI in customer operations is primarily about cutting headcount. O'Connell's respondents are overwhelmingly focused on improving net revenue retention and customer expansion. The conversation closes with O'Connell's most forward-looking observation: the coordination tax is a temporary problem that AI should eventually solve, but measuring it is the prerequisite that most enterprises are still skipping. title: How a Logistics Giant Keeps AI Data Locked Down
summary: Picture a startup with ten engineers hammering away on AI and one person lying awake over a $20,000 bill that hasn't arrived yet. That's the scenario we put to Jason Ward , who handles FinOps for AI at C.H. Robinson and recently joined the FinOps Foundation's AI working group. Jason's first answer is not glamorous: tag every AI resource so you know who owns it. The rest of the episode is what that makes possible. He walks through how C.H. Robinson runs AI across order entry, quoting, booking, and tracking, and why the team routes Anthropic models through Vertex AI to keep data locked down. Then come the metrics. Jason uses AI to dig through his own observability platform for signals he didn't know were there. One of them is how chatty a model is. That signal turned a prompt bloat alert into a bug in the code that kept retrying and burning tokens. Its opposite, context starvation, burns tokens too: a model with too little context keeps failing and trying again. We also cover why agentic and conversational workloads need separate baselines. Jason explains why cost per order is the easy win, and why most of the real work doesn't fit into neat discrete tasks. That's where his experimental cost per thought metric comes in, with reasoning ratio and cache hit rate alongside it. His advice is simple: your AI is the best tool you have for understanding your AI. title: Turning Biological Complexity into R&D Advantage with Virtual Cells - with Giorgio Gaglia of Sanofi & Daniel Veres of Turbine
summary: Drug discovery teams are running short of new ideas to test, and AI models that simulate how cells respond to drugs only pay off once leaders know when those predictions can be trusted with experiments, timelines, and budget. In this episode, Daniel Veres, Co-Founder and Chief Scientific Officer at Turbine, and Giorgio Gaglia, Head of Systems and Disease Biology at Sanofi, examine with host Yolandi de Weerdt how testing models on data they have never seen shows which R&D decisions their predictions can reliably inform. The discussion offers R&D leaders a practical way to judge when a model's predictions are ready to inform which experiments to run, where in the pipeline to start, and how much risk to accept. title: Ukraine's Secret Weapon: The Points System Winning the Drone War | Andrii Hrytseniuk
summary: Ukraine tracks every confirmed drone kill with video evidence, deduplicates the data to prevent double-counting, converts verified strikes into e-points, and delivers newly ordered weapons to frontline units in two weeks instead of twelve months. Andrii Hrytseniuk, CEO of Brave1- Ukraine's government defense innovation agency - joins Craig Smith to explain in precise operational detail how what started as a consumer loyalty program concept became the most consequential military procurement reform in modern warfare. The Army of Drones Bonus Program, running on the Delta command ecosystem with AI-assisted verification and a marketplace built like a military Amazon, has produced outcomes nobody predicted at launch: 35,000 Russian casualties per month confirmed with video evidence, the ability to change military targeting priorities instantly across an entire army by adjusting point values, and the identification of unknown high-performing frontline units whose methods are now being replicated across the force. The conversation reveals details that rarely surface in coverage of the conflict. Capturing Russian soldiers earns more bonus points than killing them, a deliberate design choice reflecting the preference not to kill when alternatives exist, and drones are actively being used to guide surrendering Russian soldiers to Ukrainian positions. The Delta ecosystem contains the world's largest military AI training dataset, already being used by defense companies to train targeting, interception, and recognition models. And perhaps most significantly: the US and France are now implementing similar marketplace and decentralized procurement approaches modeled directly on what Brave1 demonstrated works at scale. Ukraine is no longer just a recipient of military support. It is the primary laboratory for the future of warfare, and it is actively exporting what it has learned. title: Interview #94 Kamal Hathi, SVP and GM, Splunk at Cisco
summary: Kamal Hathi, SVP and GM of Splunk at Cisco, breaks down why intent is never enough to control an AI agent: agents are ruthless goal seekers, and asking one to free up 3 percent of disk space can end with 97 percent free because nobody said keep the rest. He explains why trust means verification rather than instruction, and why it includes the invoice, comparing it to hiring a contractor you trust to build a house that stands without emptying your bank account. Kamal also digs into why the rush toward air gapped and local AI is driven less by distrust of frontier labs than by cost, with specialized small models running 97 percent cheaper and 95 percent faster than frontier calls, and why the real threat is the unknown unknowns, agents nobody cataloged acting inside a state of perpetual breach. Finally, he argues agents are the new apps, and every job starts to look like a software developer's: tell the agent what to do, inspect the work, and iterate. title: From Polling to Prediction Markets: How Reliable Can We Predict Elections?
summary: This latest episode of the Harvard Data Science Review Podcast takes a closer look at election polling: how polls are conducted, what they can tell us about voters, and why measuring public opinion has become increasingly challenging. In advance of the Harvard Political Analytics 2026 conference, hosts Liberty Vittert Capito and Xiao-Li Meng are joined by two conference speakers: Anthony Salvanto, CBS News’s director of elections and surveys, and Michael A. Bailey, author of Polling at a Crossroads: Rethinking Modern Survey Research . From declining response rates and changing turnout patterns to weighting, online panels, and election-night projections, Salvanto and Bailey explore what goes on behind the numbers—and why modern pollsters are increasingly also modelers. They discuss the assumptions and human judgment embedded in polling, the importance of data quality, and the challenge of measuring and communicating uncertainty when traditional measures such as the margin of error tell only part of the story. The conversation also considers the growing role of prediction markets and what they can—and cannot—add to our understanding of elections and public opinion. Ultimately, the episode asks a larger question: In a rapidly changing polling landscape, how can researchers and the public better understand what the numbers really mean? Our guests: Michael A. Bailey is the Colonel William J. Walsh Professor of American Government in the Department of Government and McCourt School of Public Policy at Georgetown University. His research focuses on applying statistical techniques to answering questions at the intersection of political science, policy, law, and economics. Anthony Salvanto is the executive director of elections and surveys at CBS News. He oversees the CBS News Poll and all surveys across topics and heads the CBS News Decision Desk that estimates outcomes on election nights.

title: Interview #93 Hao Yang, VP and Head of AI, Splunk at Cisco
summary: Hao Yang, VP and Head of AI at Splunk, breaks down why sampling an AI system's output cannot earn trust: a fraction of ten thousand probabilistic calls will be wrong, and a spot check is unlikely to find them. He explains why a small model can grade a frontier model reliably inside a narrow context but not outside one, and why prompt injection follows from the architecture rather than being a bug, since following instructions is how these systems work. Hao also digs into why time series is still not a first class citizen in frontier models even as multimodal training reaches vision and audio, and why he rejects routing prompts to the cheapest model, arguing cost is meaningless without value. Finally, he argues against the single super agent, which by design holds access to everything it might ever need, and for guided autonomy, where an agent asks before first reaching for a tool and the user grants it once, for the session, or never. title: The Caveman Prompting Challenge
summary: Caveman prompting has one rule: why use many words when few do the trick? It saves tokens on the way in and on the way out. Push it too far, though, and the output falls apart. So how far is too far? Nobody has benchmarked it yet, and that question opens our conversation with James Barney , Head of Forward Labs at MetLife . James spends his days connecting new AI capabilities to old business problems across dozens of regulatory regimes, and he still finds time to push code. He explains how the FinOps Foundation's AI working group took on the most basic question: which model for which workload, and why the answer always comes down to cost, speed, and accuracy. We get into Anthropic's launch pricing for Fable, why a million tokens is easy to price and hard to explain, and why every stakeholder eventually tells you what they really care about once you name the wrong North Star. From there it gets practical. Start with the smartest model, then step down and add harness until quality holds. Treat exploration tokens like local builds and production tokens like pipelines. Govern agents the way you govern people, with proactive blocks, reactive checks, and policy as code an agent can actually read. We close on a bigger shift. When a chat window can pull from every dashboard at once, do we still need dashboards? James thinks mostly not, with one catch he calls the latent shopper problem: some insights only come from browsing data you did not know to ask about. title: Why AI Makes Games Worse—and How to Make Them Better
summary: Piero Molino on Player Backlash, Small Open-Weight Models, and the Economics of AI in Video Games. Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube • AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon • RSS . Piero Molino , CEO and co-founder of Studio Atelico , joins Ben Lorica to discuss what happens when AI becomes a core game mechanic rather than a cost-cutting tool. They explore why on-device, specialized models could unlock new kinds of games, how post-training gives developers greater control, why artists should share in the value created from their work, and what coding agents mean for the future of software development. Subscribe to the Gradient Flow Newsletter Interview highlights – key sections from the video version: Introduction: Why AI and Games Haven’t Clicked Yet AI as a Core Game Mechanic: The Physics-Engine Analogy and Bobium Brawlers When AI Makes Games Worse—and the Gameplay Sweet Spot The Best AI Becomes Invisible AI-Native Games, Player Adoption, and the Economics of Cloud AI AI-Generated Assets, Quality, Ethics, and Player Backlash Edge vs. Cloud: Multimodal AI Engines, Small Models, and On-Device Inference Running AI on Phones: Apple Metal, Hardware, and Efficient Kernels Post-Training Small Models to Close the Frontier-Model Gap Turning an AI Engine into a Platform for Game Developers The Device as the Deployment Boundary: Unified Memory and Scaling Up Apple, OS-Level Models, and a Hybrid Local-Cloud Future Artist Rights, Open Source, and Competition in the Game-Development Stack Coding Agents, Developer Skill, and What Still Separates the Best Small Models, World Models, and the Next Wave of Interactive Experiences Jump to transcript Related content : A video version of this conversation is available on our YouTube channel . Andrew Dai → Reasoning Doesn’t Start With Language Yoon Kim → Why Video Is AI’s Next Great Frontier David Fattal → The Missing Data for Spatial Intelligence Pete Warden → TinyML, Sensor-Driven AI, and Advances in Large Language Models Support our work by subscribing to our newsletter Transcript Below is a polished and edited transcript . Ben Lorica. All right. So today we have an old friend, Piero Molino, CEO and co-founder of Studio Atelico, which you can find at Atellico.studio. The taglines are “AI games with a human touch” and “AI tech that runs on device.” And with that, Piero, welcome to the podcast. Piero Molino. It’s so nice to chat with you again, Ben. It’s been a while, and we’re looking forward to chatting more with you about this. Ben Lorica. Actually, yeah. For our listeners who may not be aware, Piero comes from an enterprise infrastructure background. There’s the open source project Ludwig, which he created when he was at Uber AI, and which became a startup called Predibase. But now he’s in mobile and mobile games, which is fascinating and will be the focus of our conversation. Obviously, I’ll try to broaden it out so that people who are not working in mobile games will also find it interesting. But I guess, Piero, let’s start here at a high level. What do you think the AI industry gets wrong about games, and vice versa? What does the gaming industry get wrong about AI? Piero Molino. That’s a great question. When I started this company, I brought together people from both the AI industry and the gaming industry, exactly because those two spaces don’t interact a lot. In particular, it’s been surprising for me to see that gaming has been an early application of every new technology in the last 30 years. Imagine 3D physics, networking with online games, mobile games—all of these things. Whenever there was a new piece of technology, one of the first things people would implement with it would be a game. That has not been the case with AI. I think it is because of what you just said: maybe the AI people get something wrong about games, and the games people get something wrong about AI. To a certain extent, that’s what I’m trying to reconcile with the company. I’ve been doing this for about a year and a half now, so despite being relatively green in the gaming industry, I have a deep passion for games. I’ve been playing and buying games throughout the years, and some of my games have now become retro games. But when I bought them, they were not retro games. I’ve been observing the space, and I’ve been very close to it. During my college years, I was a video game journalist for a little bit, doing reviews of video games and things like that. So I’ve been following the space for a long time. For me, working on these two things together was an opportunity to bring some of my technical knowledge from the AI industry into the gaming industry, and also finally do something that has been my passion for a long time. What I’m seeing is that a lot of the gaming industry has, on one hand, been late to adopt AI technologies at the development level. I think maybe starting this year, people are really beginning to use coding agents to build games. Now you can see that whenever there’s a new model that comes out, some of the demos are always, “Oh, how well can you build this game?” or “Can I one-shot this game?” and things like that. On the other hand, there has been asset production—creating images, audio, voices, and things like that. Ben Lorica. And NPCs too, right? Piero Molino. Yeah, for NPCs. And on those things, there has been quite a bit of pushback because it seems like players feel it’s cheapening their experience instead of adding the real thing, like a human being drawing something or a human being performing some lines. It seems like AI is basically a mechanism for cheapening the development cost and cheapening their experience. I’m sympathetic to that kind of argument because games are an incredible combination of tech and art. If you make it so the art is not as good as it used to be, but it’s cheaper, then it feels like the worst version. Ben Lorica. And I guess what you’re pointing out there is that the focus is on cost reduction— Piero Molino. Exactly. Ben Lorica. —rather than actually improving the game. Piero Molino. Exactly. And that’s actually what I’m trying to do—the opposite of it. I’m trying to make it possible to use AI within the game in order to give game designers and game developers one more tool to make new games that would not have been possible before. I think a good analogy here is physics engines. If you imagine a game before physics engines were a thing, you would push a box, and your character would push it by a specified distance in the gaming world. That gave developers and designers perfect control over where the boxes were, but it didn’t allow for emergent things. Once you have a physics engine, you can use these boxes for doing puzzles, like in Portal, for instance, or other games like that. Or you can do things like building. There’s a famous game called World of Goo where you build bridges with gooey little creatures. You stick them together, and basically you create physics-based soft bodies to see if they can support the passage of some cars and things like that. Fundamentally, adding these new capabilities, like physics, enabled a set of games that were not possible before. That’s what I want to do with AI and games: give people AI tools so that they can create new games that were not possible before. Ben Lorica. So it seems like the distinction here—maybe this is an oversimplification—is between AI as a gimmick and AI actually adding something substantial to the game and the game mechanics. Piero Molino. Yeah. I want to make it a foundational piece of the game mechanics of all the games that we’re going to make, because that enables something new. I can give you a cool example. Our first game that we are developing, Bobium Brawlers, embodies these concepts and these values. It’s a game where you create your own creatures just by describing them. These creatures are represented both with images and portraits, but also by a deck of cards that you can use to battle against your friends. Both of those depend on what the player describes. If I describe a dragon that spits fire, then I’m going to do fire attacks, and the picture of the creature will be a dragon. But if I create an ice wolf, then my attacks will be more ice-oriented, and the picture will depict a wolf. Because this is done in real time, and there’s an infinite number of possibilities that players can create, it would not have been feasible to do it in any other way than having AI generate it in real time. So it becomes core to the experience. This is just an example. We’re also developing some other prototypes. This just shows what it means to have AI at the core of the gameplay. Ben Lorica. Yeah. In fact, as I recall—I may have read this somewhere—you built a bunch of prototypes, and your initial conclusion was that AI, in many instances, makes the game worse. Right? Piero Molino. Yeah. What we discovered right at the beginning was that first we created a basic technological layer, which I can tell you a little bit more about later because I think the technical aspects are also interesting for your audience. Once we built the base of that layer, we were trying to figure out what fun game mechanics that technological AI layer could enable. We created many prototypes along a spectrum, from ones where there was little to no AI—just a little sprinkle on top of a classical game mechanic—all the way to game mechanics that were, I would say, 99% AI. To give you some examples, you can imagine something that looks more or less like a board game, but where some of the pieces of the board are generated by AI. That would be an example of very little AI. Or, to think about a lot of AI, you can imagine playing Dungeons & Dragons where the AI plays the role of the game master. You tell it what happens, and it tells you how the world changes. These are the two extremes. What we found is that if you go one route—the very little AI route—it doesn’t add a lot, so it’s not particularly useful. Why would you want to have it at all? If you go to the other extreme, what happens is that it feels very gimmicky, and it doesn’t feel like a game, because games need challenge. They also need rules that the player can learn and master so they can feel like they’re getting better at it. You have some aspects of the game where AI is fundamental and the game would not have been possible before, but some other aspects where classical game mechanics and game design become the predominant part. If you blend them together, that’s what we found to be the most fun. This is how we got to Bobium Brawlers, where the creature-creation side is all AI-governed, but when you fight battles with your friends, that’s more classical game mechanics—a card-and-dice game that is more familiar to players, where they know how they can get better, how they can progress, and what challenge they have to overcome. Personally, and as a company, we rely on them. They’re a big part of our tooling. At the same time, what I’ve discovered over the last year or so, since we’ve been using them more heavily, is that the exact same tool in the hands of different developers ends up producing quite different output. I think the quality and experience of the individuals using the tools influence the results a lot. For us, it’s not going to be a mechanism to cut costs of any sort. It’s more a mechanism to be faster. With the same number of people, you can be faster, as opposed to cutting people. Ben Lorica. That statement you just made—in the hands of people who are good—but in the future, Piero, how do we know who’s good if everyone is using the same coding agents? I just talked about this with someone. In math, which is where I came from, they now have a situation where generating a proof is easy. Maybe even writing the paper is easy because you can ask the AI to write the paper. Now, whether or not the paper can be understood by mathematicians is a different thing. Mathematicians are proposing that not only is generating the proof cheap, and maybe writing the paper is also cheap, but in order for a paper to be accepted, one, it has to be understood by humans who will accept it, and secondly, they’re discussing an additional requirement. They might say, “Hey, Piero, you submitted this paper. We want you to give a talk about this paper in front of mathematicians.” In terms of coding, I guess the equivalent would be some sort of code review. That’s how you discover, “Hey, this guy is the next Jeff Dean.” Piero Molino. Yeah, that’s a great point. And I would say the role and decisions of—I think it’s like a— Ben Lorica. By the way, for coding and math, you have generation, but the verification step is also doable because you have compilers and formal verifiers. You can even have the AI do the tests. In other words, generate tests, verify, write the paper—or in the case of coding, generate the documentation. Everyone is on the same footing. So what distinguishes the star from the non-star? Piero Molino. Yeah. I think first of all it’s the “what.” Ben Lorica. Okay. Piero Molino. You have all the intelligence, quote-unquote, in what to work— Ben Lorica. On. What to work on. Piero Molino. What to work on. It’s a very important choice. It becomes the most important skill. Ben Lorica. That’s still what remains in math, unless the AI solves all of the famous problems. But then after that, what? Piero Molino. Yeah. Again, I think we’ll figure out that there are more problems. At the limit, there’s always an infinite number of problems one could be solving. Maybe it’s different between math and code, but— Ben Lorica. In math, it’s a non-renewable resource. There are only so many interesting problems. Piero Molino. At the same time, once you learn something—I’m sure this is always true in science—then you think about the consequences of what you’ve learned. Ben Lorica. This is the case when the human does it, because the human will try to solve something, get stuck, go this way, explore, do a bunch of things, and then maybe say, “Oh, there are interesting problems here too.” It’s not clear that the AI will do that. Piero Molino. Right. You can have an outer loop that is kind of self-improving, but— Ben Lorica. The human, in the course of exploring, has taste. Piero Molino. Yeah. And whenever you learn something, that changes your mental model about the world and about— Ben Lorica. Whereas the AI is just an optimization engine that’s trying to crunch through so much compute to give you the answer. Piero Molino. Yeah. But you’re directing it somehow, right? Even if you’re not directing it, you’re still creating the scaffolding that makes it so that it discovers a direction. Ben Lorica. So there’s still the “what.” What do you think about this whole notion that you should be able to explain to me what— Piero Molino. For scientific discoveries, definitely that is valuable because I think discovery without understanding—we couldn’t falsify it. Ben Lorica. It would be like Einstein saying, “I have the theory of relativity, but I cannot give a talk about it.” Piero Molino. Exactly. It’s not true knowledge if it’s not disseminated, and if we’re not able to disseminate it. I think it’s similar in a sense for coding. You, as the developer, are the first critic of this thing. The critique is super valuable. To give an example, let’s assume I’m creating a piece of code that needs to run on a device. Once it has been built, I try to run it on another device, and it breaks. Maybe I didn’t make it clear from the very beginning which devices I wanted it to run on. But after the fact, I can critique it and say, “Well, this works here, but it doesn’t work there. That’s the new task you have to do. Now you have to make it work there.” A human can also look at the generalization. My personal experience has been that these models are extremely good at writing code, and sometimes even redundant code, and sometimes making patches on top of patches on top of patches. In particular, because it’s so easy for them to write yet another piece of code, generalizing across multiple instances, multiple devices, or multiple different implementations of the same thing using design patterns is not always the first way they implement things or think about them. There’s an argument to be made that it doesn’t matter—they can create yet another bespoke function. But their memory and context are also limited. So if you create, let’s say, 100 different implementations of the same function for 100 different devices, they themselves, when something breaks, will not know where to look. I think good software design principles are something a human can provide and influence the model toward. Ben Lorica. Which, unfortunately, is somewhat gained through experience. But if you’re not gaining experience— Piero Molino. Exactly. And that’s a problem. If you are only using models from the very beginning, you don’t have the opportunity to gain that experience. That is a problem. I think maybe that’s something to be said for schools, actually. Like, why would— Ben Lorica. They need to rethink what they do and teach, right? All right. Last question to get you out of here. Obviously, because of what you do, you need to pay attention to frontier models. We talked about world models, multimodal models. Is there anything that excites you that you feel is somewhat below the radar that, in six months, more of us will be talking about? Piero Molino. Interesting. Obviously, I’m very excited about smaller models and things that run on the device and that whole space. I think some people are starting to pay more attention to it. Ben Lorica. A lot more are beginning to, right? Piero Molino. Exactly. I think there will be more of that. I’m preaching to the choir here, I’m sure, but it’s also the kind of thing I’m working on, so I’m excited about it. Of the things I’m not directly working on, I think there’s an interesting space opening up around world models. Specifically, I’m not a strong believer in, let’s say, the original formulation of world models as just: past frames plus controls equals next frame. Fundamentally, I’m not convinced by that because the inductive bias has so little structure that you would require an incredible amount of data to make it do anything reasonable. And then when there’s a bug, you don’t know what to do. If it does something different, what are you going to do? You’re going to create much, much more data to try to compensate for errors. I think it’s a recipe for not-great outcomes. But what I’m seeing is the beginning of people starting to inject some structure. So you get a blending of structures that come from game engines together with some of the techniques of world models and style transfer, et cetera. The blending of these two things, I think, is interesting and promising. Maybe not exactly for video games as we understand them today, but for potentially creating new kinds of interactive experiences that we haven’t thought about up until now. That could be interesting—more interactive-movie-style things rather than, strictly speaking, games. I’m interested in that. I think it could be fun. Ben Lorica. And with that, thank you, Piero. Always great to catch up with you. Piero Molino. Likewise, Ben. Thanks for having me. It was a pleasure chatting with you again.
summary_html:
Piero Molino on Player Backlash, Small Open-Weight Models, and the Economics of AI in Video Games.

Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube •  AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon •  RSS.

Piero Molino, CEO and co-founder of Studio Atelico, joins Ben Lorica to discuss what happens when AI becomes a core game mechanic rather than a cost-cutting tool. They explore why on-device, specialized models could unlock new kinds of games, how post-training gives developers greater control, why artists should share in the value created from their work, and what coding agents mean for the future of software development.

Subscribe to the Gradient Flow Newsletter

Interview highlights – key sections from the video version:

      1. Introduction: Why AI and Games Haven’t Clicked Yet
      2. AI as a Core Game Mechanic: The Physics-Engine Analogy and Bobium Brawlers
      3. When AI Makes Games Worse—and the Gameplay Sweet Spot
      4. The Best AI Becomes Invisible
      5. AI-Native Games, Player Adoption, and the Economics of Cloud AI
      6. AI-Generated Assets, Quality, Ethics, and Player Backlash
      7. Edge vs. Cloud: Multimodal AI Engines, Small Models, and On-Device Inference
      8. Running AI on Phones: Apple Metal, Hardware, and Efficient Kernels
      9. Post-Training Small Models to Close the Frontier-Model Gap
      10. Turning an AI Engine into a Platform for Game Developers
      11. The Device as the Deployment Boundary: Unified Memory and Scaling Up
      12. Apple, OS-Level Models, and a Hybrid Local-Cloud Future
      13. Artist Rights, Open Source, and Competition in the Game-Development Stack
      14. Coding Agents, Developer Skill, and What Still Separates the Best
      15. Small Models, World Models, and the Next Wave of Interactive Experiences
